sentences.text: Ornithomimus was a genus of ornithomimid theropod dinosaurs found in western North America during the Late Cretaceous, and it was bipedal while superficially resembling ratites.
This swift dinosaur was covered in feathers, possessed a small toothless beak, and had small skulls with light bones, suggesting they were agile and capable of high speeds.
Its very long limbs and hollow bones would have made it a swift runner, with the tibia approximately 20% longer than the femur.
The generic name means "bird imitator," derived from Greek ornis (bird) and mimos (imitator), referring to the bird-like foot.
A fourth feathered Ornithomimus specimen, described in October 2015 by Aaron van der Reest, Alex Wolfe, and Phil Currie, was the first to preserve tail feathers.
A 2012 study concluded O. edmontonicus was covered in downy feathers at all growth stages, with only adults having moderate bird-like wing structures, suggesting wings evolved for mating displays.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the length of Ornithomimus edmontonicus at 3.8 meters and its weight at 170 kilograms.

The first Ornithomimus fossil was found in 1889 and described by American paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh in 1890, based on a partial hindlimb and forelimb found by George Lyman Cannon on June 30, 1889.
The type species of Ornithomimus is Ornithomimus velox.

The diet of Ornithomimus is debated; while theropods might have been carnivorous, its body shape suggests a largely omnivorous lifestyle, and its body shape also suggests a partially or largely herbivorous lifestyle. Suggested food items include insects, crustaceans, fruits, leaves, branches, eggs, and the flesh of lizards and small mammals.
Suggested food items for Ornithomimus include insects, crustaceans, fruits, leaves, branches, eggs, and the flesh of lizards and small mammals.
Large eye sockets suggest Ornithomimus had a keen visual sense and possibly lived nocturnally, and large eye sockets suggest acute vision and the possibility that Ornithomimus was nocturnal.

A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and others examined 178 Ornithomimus foot bones for stress fractures but found none, and in a 2001 study, Bruce Rothschild and colleagues examined 178 foot bones referred to Ornithomimus for stress fractures but found none.
Ornithomimus is usually classified into two species: Ornithomimus velox and Ornithomimus edmontonicus.
Marsh initially thought Ornithomimus was an ornithopod, but this changed after Hatcher found a partial ornithomimid skeleton in Wyoming, which Marsh named O. sedens in 1892.
Gregory S. Paul classified several genera including Archaeornithomimus, Struthiomimus, Dromiceiomimus, and Gallimimus as species of Ornithomimus in 1988, though this view is not widely accepted.
Ornithomimus lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian ages of the Late Cretaceous, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
Ornithomimus lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 66 million years ago in the Maastrichtian stage, in what is now North America.
It is debated whether Coelosaurus antiquus belongs to Ornithomimus, with some researchers considering it a nomen dubium.
A 2010 re-evaluation by Lindsay Zanno and colleagues cast doubt on the assignment of a Kaiparowits Formation specimen to O. velox and possibly even to Ornithomimus.

In 1920, Charles Whitney Gilmore named O. affinis for Dryosaurus grandis based on indeterminate material, a classification that is now considered dubious, and in 1933, William Arthur Parks created O. elegans, which is now seen as belonging to Chirostenotes or Elmisaurus.
